title: A Geometric Perspective on Next-Token Prediction in Large Language Models: Three Emerging Phases (Lombardo, Trimigno, Cagnoni; arXiv 2605.09011, May 2026)
sections_read: Abstract
1 Introduction (incl. 'Our approach: lenses as geometric probes', contributions a-b)
2 Background and Related Work
2.1 Background (residual stream; representation lenses)
2.2 Related Work (mechanistic interpretability; geometric/linear structure; depth-dependent computation and phase structure)
3 Methodology
3.1 Predictive Readout Subspace and Grassmann trajectory (incl. Readout Subspace Similarity, RSS)
3.2 Phase boundaries detection (experimental setup; resolution-scale analysis and Pareto frontier; unimodality assumption; breakpoints detection)
3.3 Functional Interpretation Setup
4 Results
4.1 Phase detection (unimodality validation; phase identification and robustness; scaling laws of phase boundaries)
4.2 Geometric Characterization of the Three Phases (near-orthogonality of updates; effective rank; FFN/MHA norm ratio)
4.3 Functional Interpretation of the Three Phases (Phase 1 Seeding Multiplexing; Phase 2 Hoisting Overriding; Phase 3 Focal Convergence)
5 Discussion (Comparison with Mean-Field Theory; Conclusions; Limitations)
References
Appendix A Representation Lens Training and Experiments Setup (dataset; optimization; generalization of trained lenses; computational resources; execution time)
Appendix B Pairwise RSS Similarity Matrices Across Truncation Levels
Appendix C Pareto Frontier Between Visibility@K and Spectral Energy
Appendix D Unimodality Validation and Phase Detection Across All Models
Appendix D.1 Breakpoints detection
Appendix E Geometric Characterization of the Three Phases: Full Results (RSS profiles and consensus breakpoints; near-orthogonality of updates; effective rank of hidden states and layer updates)

setup.data: Lens training: 226.49M tokens from SlimPajama (CommonCrawl 130.33M, C4 65.72M, ArXiv 11.52M, GitHub 9.66M, StackExchange 7.31M, Wikipedia 1.95M; Table 1). All input-dependent metrics use 16M tokens from a held-out SlimPajama validation subset (Table 1 lists 18.66M eval tokens). Generic next-token prediction on web/code text. No task data, no factual QA, no failure or pressure conditions.
setup.models: Two families (base checkpoints inferred from the names; the paper never says base vs instruct): Qwen2.5-1.5B, 7B, 14B, 32B and OLMo-2-1B, 7B, 13B, 32B (16 to 64 layers). The OLMo-2 checkpoints (named only in Figure 14 titles) are OLMo-2-0425-1B, OLMo-2-1124-7B, OLMo-2-1124-13B and OLMo-2-0325-32B, i.e. three different release dates. OLMo-2 uses a different block design (the paper calls it 'parallel').
setup.layers_positions: Every layer. Readout subspace S_l^(k) = span of the top-k right singular vectors of the tuned-lens correction matrix A_l (h~ = (I + A_l) h + b_l), for k in {1, 3, 5, 10, 15, 25, 35, 50}% of d. Functional metrics use the residual h_l and the total update Delta_l = Delta_MHA + Delta_FFN at every token position, averaged over tokens and batches.
setup.method_in_one_line: Train a TunedLens per layer, SVD its correction matrix, treat the top-k right singular subspace as a point on Gr(k, d), and track the mean cosine of principal angles between consecutive layers (RSS); find two breakpoints in that profile and characterise the three resulting phases with Hit@k, effective rank, |cos(update, residual)| and the FFN/MHA norm ratio.
setup.baselines: LogitLens (A_l = 0) against the tuned representation lens for Hit@k. For the profile shape: four parametric fits (Beta, generalized normal, asymmetric generalized normal, Kumaraswamy).
setup.controls: Held-out validation tokens for all input-dependent metrics; per-layer train vs validation distillation loss (Figure 14, gaps +0.012 to +0.089); sweep over k with consensus breakpoints over k in {5, 10, 15}% and stability check at out-of-regime k (sigma <= 3.9%); two architecture families. Missing: any causal intervention; any null baseline for RSS (e.g. random or shuffled lens matrices); any item- or condition-level comparison.
setup.compute: Two NVIDIA L40S (48 GB) GPUs, two Xeon Gold 6430 CPUs, 1 TB RAM. Lens training from a few hours (1B) to about four days (32B); evaluation from a few hours to about 1.5 days (32B). Lens training: AdamW, lr 1e-3, 500 steps, 50 warmup, 2^18 tokens per step (about 131M tokens in total, less than the 226.49M-token training set, so lenses see a subset; the paper does not say which); official tuned-lens code.

key_results.claim: A tuned (affine) lens decodes the final token from the earliest layers, while the logit lens is near zero until the last phase: the information is present but not yet in the output basis.
key_results.quote: The representation lens recovers the final token early, while the LogitLens remains nearly blind until the final phase, indicating predictive information is present but hidden in superposition.

key_results.claim: Even at layer 1, tuned-lens Hit@1 is about 0.3 and Hit@5 about twice that.
key_results.quote: Already at layer 1, Hit@1 is ≈ 0.28–0.33 and Hit@5/Hit@1 ≈ 2.0, indicating the final token is among the top candidates from the earliest layers but not yet dominant.

key_results.claim: The consecutive-layer similarity of the lens readout subspace splits depth into three phases; the middle phase takes most of the depth.
key_results.quote: On average, Phase 1 spans 19.8% ± 6.9%, Phase 2 59.0% ± 12.4%, and Phase 3 21.2% ± 8.6%, with the intermediate phase dominating.

key_results.claim: Breakpoints are stable when k is changed outside the 5-15% band used to set them.
key_results.quote: Comparing with breakpoints at out-of-regime k ∈ 1%, 3%, 25%, 35%, 50% shows tightly concentrated estimates (σ ≤ 3.9%; Figure 8), indicating stable boundaries.

key_results.claim: Deeper models spend the extra layers mainly in Phase 2 (P2 width slope 0.89 Qwen, 0.62 OLMo). The authors' 'Phases 1 and 3 remain roughly constant' holds for Qwen2.5 only: in OLMo-2, b1 grows 4, 9, 9, 17 layers for 1B-32B (slope 0.26, R2 0.97; 23-29% of depth throughout) and Phase 3 grows 7, 6, 8, 12 layers (Figures 6, 8).
key_results.quote: Overall, as depth increases, Phase 2 expands while Phases 1 and 3 remain roughly constant.

key_results.claim: Authors' claim (abstract), partly contradicted by their own Figures 12, 20, 21: phases are told apart by what updates do to effective rank, not by alignment with the residual stream. In fact |cos(update, residual)| (about 0.02-0.4) also splits by phase (lowest in Phase 2 in 7/8 models, highest in Phase 3 in a claimed 8/8), and hidden-state rank does not 'concentrate' in Phase 3 (flat, or rising in all four Qwen2.5 models); only update rank and norm concentrate (Figures 9, 22).
key_results.quote: Updates are approximately orthogonal to the residual stream throughout; what distinguishes the phases is their effect on the effective rank, which expands, stabilizes, and concentrates.

key_results.claim: Phase 2: the tuned lens concentrates on one candidate while the logit lens still cannot read it.
key_results.quote: Hit@1 rises to ≈ 0.56 and Hit@5/Hit@1 decreases, showing progressive concentration, while LogitLens remains low (≈ 0.03–0.10), implying disambiguation within the subspace without explicit decoding.

key_results.claim: The paper's (interpretive) account of Phase 2 as candidate competition.
key_results.quote: one candidate is progressively lifted above the others (hoisting) by overriding competing subspaces (overriding), without altering the established predictive geometry.

key_results.claim: Phase 3: the output basis catches up with the tuned lens; the winner becomes readable.
key_results.quote: The Hit@5/Hit@1 ratio drops (≈ 1.2–1.5) while LogitLens Hit@1 rises (≈ 0.30–0.50), approaching the representation lens, indicating the final token is directly readable.

key_results.claim: Phase 3 updates are large and low-rank.
key_results.quote: update norms grow sharply (up to 10×), concentrating on few high-energy directions within the predictive subspace

key_results.claim: Block-level split: Qwen2.5 Phase 1 is FFN-heavy; OLMo-2 more balanced.
key_results.quote: In Phase 1, families differ: QWEN2.5 is FFN-dominated (ratio 2.4–3.2) while OLMO2 shows more balanced updates due to its parallel design

key_results.claim: FFN writes the final prediction in Phase 3 in both families.
key_results.quote: Contributions are more balanced in Phase 2, and FFN dominates across both families in Phase 3, suggesting activation of distributed memories to write the final prediction into the residual stream.

key_results.claim: The three-phase shape is not an artifact of forcing a unimodal fit.
key_results.quote: Importantly, more flexible families (Beta, Kumaraswamy) do not outperform unimodal ones (GNorm, AGNorm).

methods.name: Predictive readout subspace on Gr(k, d) and Readout Subspace Similarity (RSS)
methods.what_it_measures: Per layer, the span of the top-k right singular vectors of the tuned-lens correction matrix A_l (where the lens corrects the residual most). RSS = mean cosine of the k principal angles between consecutive layers' subspaces (1 = same, 0 = orthogonal); also a full layer-by-layer matrix M(k).
methods.which_fate_it_could_diagnose: As defined, none: it is computed from lens weights only, so every input gets the same profile and flipped and resisted items cannot be compared. Adapted to condition-level subspaces (e.g. top PCs of item residuals, or of a correct-vs-claimed contrast, under neutral vs pushback at the same layer), the same principal-angle similarity could separate 5 transformed (subspace rotated but present) from 6 erased (subspace gone) and locate where the two conditions fork.
methods.causal_followup_it_allows: None in the paper. For us: patch the pushback-condition component inside the neutral-condition subspace (or project it out) at the layer where the RSS between conditions drops, and check whether the answer flips back.
methods.data_and_compute_needed: A tuned lens per layer (tuned-lens repo; hours for 1B, about 4 days for 32B on 2 L40S with 226M tokens) plus SVD of d x d matrices. The adapted version needs only cached residuals at the answer position for a few hundred items per condition and SVD/principal angles (seconds).
methods.code_available: Uses the official tuned-lens code (github.com/AlignmentResearch/tuned-lens). No code of their own is linked.

methods.name: Visibility@k vs retained energy E(k) Pareto, used to pick the subspace dimension
methods.what_it_measures: Visibility = p95 - p5 of off-diagonal pairwise similarities (contrast between layers); E(k) = share of squared singular values kept by top-k. Large k keeps energy but makes all subspaces look alike.
methods.which_fate_it_could_diagnose: None directly; it is a rule for choosing k so that principal-angle comparisons are neither noise (tiny k) nor trivially similar (huge k).

methods.name: Double-chord (two-stage Kneedle) breakpoint detection on a smoothed layer profile
methods.what_it_measures: Two knees b1 < b2 of a Gaussian-smoothed (sigma = 2) profile, one in each half of depth; consensus by mode over k in {5, 10, 15}%.
methods.which_fate_it_could_diagnose: Any fate signal that is a layer profile (e.g. correct-answer rank under a tuned lens, between-condition RSS) can be cut into 'before divergence / divergence / after' with the same tool, giving a reproducible 'where' for a fork. It assumes one knee per half, so it will miss forks that are not shaped that way.
methods.causal_followup_it_allows: Choose the layer band for patching, ablation or a layer-restricted fix.
methods.code_available: Kneedle is standard (Satopaa et al. 2011); paper code not released.

methods.name: Tuned lens vs logit lens Hit@k per layer (and Hit@5/Hit@1)
methods.what_it_measures: How often the final token is in the top-k of a per-layer learned affine readout vs the fixed unembedding readout. The gap is 'present in the residual but not yet in the output basis'.
methods.which_fate_it_could_diagnose: 1 readout/threshold failure and, with care, 4 override: per item, track the tuned-lens rank of the correct answer and of the user's claimed answer across layers. A crossing in Phase 2 (middle band) fits candidate competition/override; correct answer leading until Phase 3 and losing only there fits a late readout/commitment failure. Note the lens is trained to predict the model's own final output, so it reads 'what the model would say', not correctness.
methods.causal_followup_it_allows: Activation patching of the neutral-condition residual into the pushback run at the crossing layer; or steering along the lens-mapped contrast direction (I + A_l)^T (w_correct - w_claimed).
methods.data_and_compute_needed: One tuned lens per layer for the target model (or reuse public tuned lenses where they exist); one forward pass per item with cached residuals.

methods.name: Update geometry: |cos(Delta_l, h_{l-1})|, effective rank of H_l and Delta_l, update norm
methods.what_it_measures: How aligned each layer's write is with the existing residual, how many dimensions hidden states and updates use, and how large updates are, averaged over tokens.
methods.which_fate_it_could_diagnose: Weak, and only if computed per item and per condition: a pushback item whose late update is large and aligned against the correct-answer direction suggests 4 override; a drop in effective rank of the item cloud under pushback could hint at 6 erased/collapse. Averaged over all tokens, as in the paper, it says nothing about fates.
methods.causal_followup_it_allows: Ablate or rescale the large Phase 3 updates (FFN outputs) in pushback items and see whether the correct answer returns.
methods.data_and_compute_needed: Cached residuals and per-layer MHA/FFN outputs; cheap.

methods.name: FFN/MHA update norm ratio per phase
methods.what_it_measures: Which sublayer type writes more into the residual in each phase.
methods.which_fate_it_could_diagnose: Localisation aid only: points to MLPs for Phase 3 commitments and to mixed attention/MLP in Phase 2. For pushback, attention reading the user turn is the obvious suspect for override; this ratio can check whether the flip-relevant write is attention- or MLP-borne.
methods.causal_followup_it_allows: Sublayer-specific patching (attention-out vs MLP-out) at the fork layer.
methods.data_and_compute_needed: Hooks on attention and MLP outputs; cheap.

controls_worth_copying: Fit any learned readout (lens or probe) on one split and compute every geometric metric on held-out data; report the per-layer train vs validation gap (their Figure 14).
Sweep the subspace dimension k, show the Visibility vs energy trade-off, and set breakpoints by consensus over a middle k band with a stability check at outer k values.
Always report the learned readout next to the fixed output readout (tuned lens vs logit lens) at every layer; the gap is the measurable form of 'decodable but not yet readable'.
Test a shape assumption against more flexible alternatives before building on it (their unimodal vs Beta/Kumaraswamy check).
Run the same pipeline on two families with different block designs (they use Qwen2.5 and OLMo-2) before calling a pattern general.

pitfalls.pitfall: Breakpoints move by a few layers with the choice of k.
pitfalls.quote: Breakpoint estimates may vary by 1–3 layers across values of k due to residual noise.

pitfalls.pitfall: Subspace dimension matters: too small is noisy, too large makes all layers look alike.
pitfalls.quote: intermediate values k ∈ {5%, 10%, 15%} balance spectral energy and geometric contrast, while smaller k are noisier and larger k oversmooth.

pitfalls.pitfall: The readout subspace comes from lens weights only. It is input-independent: one trajectory per model, so it cannot compare items, prompts or conditions. Any fate use needs a subspace built from activations of the items themselves.

A tuned lens is distilled toward the model's own final distribution. On items where the model flips, it decodes the model's eventual (wrong) answer, not the correct one. Use it to locate when the output commits, and use a separate correctness probe (plus the logit-margin control) for 'decodable'.
Lenses were trained on SlimPajama web text. Chat-formatted pushback prompts are out of distribution; check lens KL on our prompts or retrain the lens on our format.
Hit@k is averaged over all tokens of web text, dominated by easy and frequent tokens; layer-1 Hit@1 of about 0.3 is unlikely to hold for factual answer tokens.

Absolute RSS changes are small (about 0.1-0.2 across depth, Figures 10 and 19); the normalized plots in Figures 4 and 18 make the rise-plateau-descent look sharper than it is. There is no null (random or shuffled lens) baseline for RSS.

Several text claims are looser than the figures: OLMo-2-1B |cos| is highest in Phase 2, not Phase 3 (Figure 20); Qwen hidden-state rank rises in Phase 3 (Figure 21); Figure 5 omits Qwen2.5-7B; Figure 18 lacks the breakpoint panels its caption describes; the Qwen2.5 citation [21] points to the Qwen3 report.

The Hit@k target is undefined: the paper never says whether 'final token' is the data's next token or the model's own final-layer top-1. Last-layer tuned-lens Hit@1 of about 0.8 vs logit-lens about 0.43 for the same layer, and 0.8 being far above plausible web-text next-token accuracy, favour 'agreement with the model's own output' (inferred). Our per-item proposals assume this reading.
pitfalls.quote: how often the final token appears in the top-k at each layer
pitfalls.source: stated definition; interpretation is our reading

limitations_quote: Phase interpretations are based on correlational evidence without causal interventions; activation patching or causal mediation analyses could provide stronger mechanistic grounding.
future_work_quote: Our analysis is restricted to two decoder-only families with dense attention and standard residual connections; extension to MoE, state-space, or non-residual architectures is left to future work.

bears_on_fates.how: The tuned-lens vs logit-lens gap is a direct, layer-resolved measure of information that is in the residual but not yet in the output basis. Per item, a correct answer that leads under the tuned lens through the middle band but loses only in Phase 3 (where lens and logit lens converge) would point to a late readout or commitment failure. The paper shows the general pattern on generic text only; it has no failure items.

Phase 2 ('hoisting overriding') is described as one candidate being lifted over competitors without changing the subspace, which is the shape an override by the user's claimed answer would take. A rank crossing of correct vs claimed answer inside Phase 2 would be the test. In the paper 'overriding' is an interpretation from correlational metrics, not a measured competition.

Principal angles between subspaces are the right tool to ask whether the answer subspace is rotated rather than gone, but the paper compares lens subspaces only across adjacent layers of one model, never across conditions, and does no Procrustes alignment.
Effective rank of hidden states could in principle show compression of an item cloud, but the paper averages over all tokens and has no item-level test.
Not addressed: no interventions of any kind.

bears_on_group_angle: This is a clean, cheap template for a Grassmann trajectory across layers: SVD, then a top-k subspace per layer, then principal angles, then mean cosine (RSS) between consecutive layers plus a full pairwise matrix, with k set from a Visibility vs energy trade-off and phase boundaries from Kneedle knees. Its weakness for us is the object: a lens-weight subspace that is the same for every input. For fates we would keep the machinery and swap the object for item- or condition-level subspaces (e.g. top PCs of answer-position residuals, or of the correct-vs-claimed contrast, under neutral vs pushback), then compare (a) the same layer across conditions (where do paths fork, rotated vs gone) and (b) consecutive layers within a condition (speed). It also says nothing about manifold vs linear steering. Cross-paper: its late 'reorientation toward the unembedding' (Phase 3) is directionally consistent with 2605.12714, where decoder models have their curvature peak late (normalized depth 0.78-0.89); qualitative only, since the objects (lens-weight subspace on web text vs example-cloud PCA subspace on MTEB inputs) and statistics (RSS decline vs curvature peak) differ. Cited leads for the manifold-vs-linear angle (not read): Gurnee et al. 2026 [10] (transformers build and manipulate low-dimensional manifolds), Shai et al. [18] (belief-state geometry in the residual stream), Bruno et al. [5] (three phases in mean-field transformers) and LoRA-Lens [20] (same authors; low-rank lenses).
architecture_location: Phase bands as depth fractions: Phase 1 ends at 11-29% of depth, Phase 3 starts at 60-89% (Figure 8). Two models in our affordable range are covered directly: Qwen2.5-14B (b1 about layer 5, b2 about layer 40; P1/P2/P3 = 5/35/7) and Qwen2.5-32B (b1 about layer 8 = 13%, b2 about layer 56 = 89%; 8/48/7). Convention: RSS_l compares layers l and l+1, so b1, b2 and these widths count transitions (they sum to L-1); e.g. Qwen2.5-14B Phase 3 starts at transition 40 to 41 and runs to the output (7 transitions, 8 layers, which is the 8 shown in Figure 6). FFN writes more than attention in Phase 3 in all 8 models (ratio about 2-3.8, approx from Figure 7), and Qwen2.5 Phase 1 is also FFN-heavy (2.4-3.2). Reading: candidate competition happens in the middle ~60% of depth; final commitment in the last ~10-20%, mostly FFN-driven.
actionable_fix: None proposed; the paper is descriptive and correlational. What it enables for us (our proposals, untested): (1) a layer coordinate system for Stage A, locating per item where the correct-vs-claimed rank crossing happens (Phase 2 vs Phase 3); (2) for Stage B, if flips concentrate in Phase 3, restrict the fix to late FFN blocks (late-layer steering or LoRA on Phase 3 MLPs) and recheck whether the middle-band tuned-lens readout of the correct answer is intact (fixed vs only hidden); if flips happen in Phase 2, target the middle band and attention reading the user turn.
reuse_verdict: Reuse partly. Reuse: tuned-lens vs logit-lens per-layer rank curves as a per-item readout trace; the published phase bands for Qwen2.5-14B and 32B as a WHERE axis; the RSS/principal-angle, Visibility-vs-k and Kneedle recipe for any layer profile we build. Do not reuse as-is: RSS on lens weights, which is input-independent and cannot separate fates or items.
relevance_to_project: Low as direct evidence, medium as a toolkit. It has no failures, pressure, facts or causal tests, and its main object is the same for every input, so it cannot tell flipped from resisted items. Its value is the tuned-lens vs logit-lens gap as a layer-resolved 'decodable but not yet readable' measure, ready phase bands for Qwen2.5-14B/32B, and a principal-angle similarity recipe we can point at condition-level subspaces instead.
